messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier had been a cashier at the same grocery store in downtown Baltimore for twenty-three years, long enough that most of his regulars knew his name and his story—or at least the version he used to tell. He was seventy-six now, a widower of eight years, and until recently he had taken quiet pride in the precision of his work: the way he could bag six items in a single motion, the way he remembered which customers liked their eggs double-bagged and which ones wanted their bread on top. That was before the memory started coming back not as a story he could tell, but as something that happened to him, again, in the middle of the checkout line.

The event itself had taken place in 1992, during the Siege of Sarajevo, where Javier had been working as a relief coordinator for a small humanitarian organization. He had been born in the United States to Spanish immigrant parents, but he had felt a pull to go, to help, to prove something to himself about what kind of man he was. One afternoon, his convoy was stopped at a checkpoint that was not supposed to be there. He remembered the crack of the rifle, the way the glass in the driver’s side window turned into a white spiderweb before it fell inward, the warm wetness on his neck that he later learned was the driver’s blood. He had lain on the floor of the van for what felt like hours, listening to the shouting in a language he half-understood, certain that at any moment the door would open and he would be next. He was not injured. He was not taken. But something in him had never really left that floor.

For decades, he managed. He returned to the States, married, raised two daughters, worked the register, went to Mass on Sundays. He told himself the war was behind him, that he had been lucky, that other people had suffered far worse. But after his wife died, the old vigilance crept back. Now, in the checkout aisle, Javier found himself scanning customers not for their groceries but for their hands—watching for anything that could become a weapon, a sudden movement, a pocket that might hold more than a wallet. He had become certain, without quite being able to say when it started, that the world was a dangerous place, and that he was no longer the man who could navigate it. The thought arrived fully formed, as if it had always been true: he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him.

The driving was the first thing to go. He stopped getting behind the wheel after a morning in June when, pulling out of his driveway, he saw a delivery truck idling at the corner and felt his chest clamp shut. The truck was just a truck, but in that moment it was the armored vehicle from the checkpoint, and his hands were shaking so badly he had to pull over. He told his daughter he was getting too old for the road, that his eyes weren’t what they used to be. But the truth was he could not bear being inside a vehicle at all—not driving, not riding as a passenger. The bus was worse, because he could not control who sat next to him, could not see what they were holding. So he walked. He walked two miles to the grocery store every morning, rain or heat, because walking meant he could see everything coming.

At work, he had developed a system. He kept his back to the wall. He scanned the aisles over the heads of customers. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him—the way a man adjusted his jacket, the way a woman held her purse too tightly. He knew, intellectually, that these were ordinary people buying milk and bread. But his body did not believe it. His body believed that danger was imminent, that he needed to stay alert, and so he did, even when it exhausted him. He had difficulty falling asleep at night because he needed to stay alert, and when he finally did sleep, he woke at the smallest sound—a car door, a creaking floorboard—his heart already pounding, his mind already running through the exits.

He had lost his faith somewhere along the way, though he could not pinpoint the moment. It was not a dramatic renunciation; it was more like a quiet evaporation. He still went to Mass because his wife had loved it, and because the ritual was familiar, but he no longer believed that anyone was listening. He thought often about why the event had happened to him, why he had been spared when the driver had not, what it meant that he had gone on to live a full life while so many others had not. He did not arrive at answers. He arrived only at a kind of hollow bewilderment.

Sometimes, when a customer asked him a question or when a child dropped a jar in the next aisle, a memory would surface—not as a thought, but as a picture, a vivid image of the shattered windshield or the pattern of blood on the driver’s shirt. He could see it perfectly, in color, and yet he felt nothing. He felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger, as if the man on that floor was someone else entirely. And then, without warning, the numbness would disappear and he would be back inside the moment—the smell of diesel and copper, the weight of the body pressed against his, the certainty that he was about to die. It was happening right now, even though it was thirty years ago.

He had started pushing away positive emotions because they felt unsafe. When his granddaughter hugged him, he felt a flash of warmth and then a wave of something like dread, as if happiness itself were a trap, as if letting himself feel good meant letting his guard down. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing keeping him alive, and that to relax was to invite disaster.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a panic attack in the middle of a Wednesday afternoon shift. A customer had dropped a glass bottle of olive oil, and the sound of it shattering on the linoleum had sent Javier to his knees behind the register, his hands over his ears, his breath coming in short, ragged gasps. His manager had called his daughter, who had driven him home—he could not get in the car, so she had walked with him, slowly, for two miles—and then she had made an appointment. He sat in the waiting room now, his hands folded in his lap, staring at the floor. He was terrified of what it would mean to talk about these things, to let them out into the light. But he was also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that someone could tell him how to stop living inside that van.
